title: The Second Head: from a Don Farmstead to Vagankovskoye, by way of Every Organ
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Don Farmstead and the Tractor Plant

stops.name: Khutor Kulikovsky, born under two calendars
stops.date_confidence: attested; 31 July 1916 New Style per en.wikipedia, 18 July Old Style per ru.wikipedia, and Konstantinov 2009 independently gives 18 July. Coordinates are the gazetteered position of khutor Kulikovsky, Novonikolaevsky District, Volgograd Oblast (50 deg 50' 15" N, 42 deg 32' 40" E); the figures carried in earlier notes, 49.9/42.0 and 50.2/42.75, are 110 km and 72 km wrong respectively.
stops.campa: A son is born on a khutor in the Don Cossack lands, a scatter of farmsteads under the stanitsa of Yaryzhenskaya, in the last summer before the empire ends. The registers hold him twice, by two reckonings: the eighteenth of July by the old style, the thirty-first by the new. His people are peasants working steppe soil between the Buzuluk and the Khoper. He will handle engines for years before he handles a scalpel. Nothing in the place suggests surgery, and for a hundred versts around, the nearest thing to a laboratory is a smithy.
suggested_refs: Khutor Kulikovsky, Novonikolaevsky District, Volgograd Oblast, which lists him as its notable native
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009), PMC2763473

stops.name: The Don country, the father killed in the civil war
stops.date_confidence: year approximate: the sources say only that Pyotr Yakovlevich died in the Russian Civil War when his son was about three. Neither ru.wikipedia nor Konstantinov states where he fell, so the pin is the family's khutor and not the place of death.
stops.campa: Pyotr Yakovlevich Demikhov is killed in the fighting that runs back and forth across the Don country while the boy is about three. The record does not say where he falls or on which side he is counted. The son who never remembers his father's face will spend fifty years cutting into hearts that are still beating. Domnika Aleksandrovna is left with three children and a farmstead, and she keeps all three in schooling, which on the Don in 1919 is a decision with consequences. All three take degrees.
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Stalingrad Tractor Plant, the mechanic at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia); month not recorded. Coordinates corrected to the plant site in Traktorozavodsky District per OSM, the earlier 48.85/44.5333 falling in the Volga floodplain northwest of the works.
stops.campa: At fifteen he leaves school for the tractor plant on the northern edge of Stalingrad, itself only three years old and already the largest machine-building works in the country. He is put to fitting and repair. The work teaches him what his critics will later call the wrong training for a surgeon and his admirers the right one: how a mechanism comes apart, and how to make by hand a part that does not exist anywhere. He will build his own instruments for the rest of his working life, filing and grinding them himself at the bench.
suggested_refs: The Stalingrad Tractor Plant, Traktorozavodsky District, built 1930

stops.name: Voronezh State University, the enrollment two sources deny
stops.date_confidence: contested and unresolved. en.wikipedia: 'In 1934, Demikhov began studying at the Voronezh State University', with no transfer year given afterward. ru.wikipedia and Konstantinov 2009 both put him at Moscow State University from 1934 and never mention Voronezh. Month is conventional. Coordinates are the university's historic city-center premises near Universitetskaya ploshchad; OSM resolves the modern entry to 51.7050, 39.1852.
stops.campa: English Wikipedia sends him here in the autumn of 1934, to Voronezh State University, and lets him transfer to Moscow later without ever saying when. The Russian article and Konstantinov's tribute both have him in Moscow from that same autumn and never mention Voronezh at all. The two accounts cannot both stand, and nothing reachable adjudicates them. What is agreed is the year and the subject: a mechanic out of a tractor plant enrolls to study physiology, and inside three years he is building an apparatus to replace a heart. In which city he sat down to do it, the record does not say.
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow State University, the physiology department on Mokhovaya
stops.date_confidence: 1934 per ru.wikipedia and Konstantinov 2009; en.wikipedia gives no transfer year at all, so an earlier note's range of 1937-1940 for this stop was invented and is discarded here. Coordinates are the old university building, Mokhovaya 11.
stops.campa: The old university building on Mokhovaya Street, across the road from the Kremlin gardens, houses the biology faculty and its physiology department. He arrives either in 1934 or at some later date the sources decline to fix. What the department teaches him is circulation: pressures, volumes, the timing of a pump made of muscle. What he wants to know is whether the pump can be swapped out, and how long a body will tolerate the substitution. The discipline he is walking into has no name yet in any language. He will coin the name himself: transplantology.
suggested_refs: The old MSU building, Mokhovaya 11, seat of the biology faculty before the Sparrow Hills campus
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow, the pump built by a third-year student
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not attested fact, and the venue is contested. ru.wikipedia: a hand-built artificial heart implanted in a dog that lived about two hours. en.wikipedia places the same 1937 device at Voronezh. Konstantinov 2009 contradicts the implantation outright, describing a mechanical assist pump too large to go inside a dog, which maintained circulation for roughly five hours after the animal's heart was excised. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: In his third year he builds, by hand, a machine to drive blood. The tradition says he puts it inside a dog and the animal lives about two hours. Konstantinov's account says the device was far too large to go inside a dog at all, and instead held the circulation up for some five hours after the animal's own heart had been cut out. Both versions agree the thing worked, and that a student made it out of nothing. The earliest paper trace of the first artificial heart is a notice in a university newspaper, printed in April 1938.
suggested_refs: The April 1938 university newspaper notice, earliest documentary trace of the 1937 device
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow State University, the degree in biology
stops.date_confidence: attested: both Wikipedias give 1940, en.wikipedia gives August. Day not recorded.
stops.campa: He takes his degree with honors from the biology faculty in August. Six years of physiology, one homemade circulatory pump, and no medical diploma whatever: he is a biologist, and a biologist he will remain to the end. The surgery he is about to invent will be carried into human chests by men holding licenses that were never issued to him, in countries he will not be allowed to visit. He never qualifies to operate on a human being, and he never does. Every incision of his working life is made in an animal, on a bench, in a room with a drain in the floor.

stops.name: Moscow, called up from the laboratory
stops.date_confidence: year attested (both Wikipedias); month unrecorded. No reachable source names a single wartime posting, town, unit, or front, so this pin marks Moscow at the point of call-up and is not a place of service.
stops.campa: The new graduate is conscripted. He spends the war as a senior laboratory technician in a pathological-anatomy laboratory attached to the active army, and as a forensic expert: bodies, sections, causes of death, written up at speed under field conditions for four years. The anatomy he learns in those years is the anatomy of the recently killed, examined in quantity, and he comes out of it knowing the inside of a chest better than most men who hold surgical degrees. No source reachable here names one town he was posted to.

stops.name: Manchuria, forensic work in the last campaign
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. en.wikipedia alone reports service in China after the Soviet declaration of war on Japan, naming no town and no month; August is the campaign's opening. The coordinates are Harbin, an acknowledged placeholder for a theater the size of western Europe, not an attested posting.
stops.campa: With the Soviet declaration of war on Japan he moves east into the Manchurian theater, still doing forensic work, still writing up the dead. English Wikipedia is the only source for the posting and it names no town, no unit, and no month; the pin here is Harbin, standing in for a campaign that crossed a territory the size of western Europe in three weeks. This is the farthest he will travel for a very long time, and the borders close behind him almost as soon as he is through them. He comes home decorated at twenty-nine.

stops.name: Moscow State University, back in the physiology department
stops.date_confidence: contested. An earlier reading had him joining the Institute of Experimental and Clinical Surgery in 1945; en.wikipedia has him resuming his post in the MSU human physiology department after the war and moving to the Institute of Surgery only in 1947, and Konstantinov 2009 gives 1947-1955 there under Vishnevsky. Month conventional for 'end of 1945'.
stops.campa: Demobilized at the end of the year, he returns to the human physiology department at Moscow State University and not to any surgical institute. The Russian account puts him inside the Institute of Experimental and Clinical Surgery from 1945; the English account and Konstantinov both keep him at the university until 1947. The distinction is not pedantic. The operations of 1946 are the ones the whole field afterward dates from, and the two accounts put them in different buildings. He resumes work with dogs, in a physiology laboratory, without a surgical team around him.
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow State University, the heart and lungs moved together
stops.date_confidence: day attested by Konstantinov 2009 for the heart-lung dog surviving 9.5 hours; both Wikipedias give 1946 for the first intrathoracic heterotopic heart transplant and an early heart-lung replacement without a day. Venue corrected to MSU: an earlier reading sited these at the Institute of Experimental and Clinical Surgery, where he was not yet working.
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of June he takes out the heart and lungs of a dog together, as one block, and puts another animal's in their place. The dog lives nine and a half hours. In the same year he performs the first intrathoracic heterotopic heart transplant, setting a second heart into a chest alongside the first and letting the two beat together in one circulation. He works fast because speed is the only thing he has. There is no heart-lung machine anywhere on earth yet, no immunosuppression, and no tissue typing he can trust.
stops.quote: The extra heart took over half the work of circulating the blood.
stops.quote_source: Demikhov's own description of the second-heart operation, published eight years later in a Stockholm communist newspaper, 25 September 1954; CIA translation CIA-RDP80-00809A000700200220-3
suggested_refs: Christiaan Barnard's 1997 letter to Konstantinov, which fixes on exactly this: 'having done all the research before extracorporeal circulation'
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow, the marriage to Liya Nikolayevna
stops.date_confidence: month attested (en.wikipedia); day not recorded. No venue is named in any reachable source, so the coordinates are a declared city-level placeholder.
stops.campa: He marries Liya Nikolayevna in August, two months after the heart-lung dog lived nine and a half hours. Nothing about the wedding survives in any reachable source beyond the month and her name: no venue, no witnesses, no photograph, no account of how they met. Her name enters the record once, on a marriage line, and does not appear in it again. She keeps the household through half a century of a career that pays badly, attracts official suspicion, and fills the flat with the smell of a laboratory. What she thought of any of it went unwritten.

stops.name: Moscow, the birth of Olga
stops.date_confidence: month attested (both Wikipedias); day not recorded. No maternity hospital named, so the coordinates are a declared city-level placeholder.
stops.campa: A daughter, Olga, is born in July. She grows up in a house where the experimental dogs have names as well as case numbers, and where the working day ends whenever the animal stabilizes. She becomes a physician and a professor in her turn, holding the medical qualification her father was never issued and never sought. No maternity hospital is named in any reachable source, so the pin is the middle of Moscow and stands for the city rather than for any address in it.

segments.name: Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya: Working Down the List

stops.name: Institute of Experimental and Clinical Surgery, the lung
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia; Konstantinov 2009 gives 1947-1955 under Vishnevsky); month not recorded. Coordinates corrected to Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya 27 per OSM, roughly 550 m northeast of the figure carried in earlier notes.
stops.campa: He moves to the Institute of Experimental and Clinical Surgery on Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya, under Vishnevsky, and for the first time has an institute's resources behind him. In the same year he performs the first isolated lung transplant in a dog. The programme he sets himself is a list rather than a question: heart, lung, heart and lung together, liver, kidney, adrenal gland, limb, head. He means to work down it organ by organ and settle, for each one, whether a transplanted organ can be made to work.
suggested_refs: The Institute of Experimental and Clinical Surgery of the USSR Academy of Medical Sciences, ancestor of the Vishnevsky Institute, Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya 27
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya, the liver
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both Wikipedias as the first experimental liver transplant; month not recorded and no case series is reachable.
stops.campa: He transplants a liver into a dog, the first attempt anywhere. The liver is the worst of the abdominal organs to move: its blood arrives from two directions, its tolerance for warm ischaemia is short, and its failure is not survivable. The technical description he leaves behind will be printed, and then translated into three languages, before any human liver is lifted out of one body and put into another. The dogs do not live long. He records what killed them, redesigns the anastomoses, and does it again.

stops.name: Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya, the heart in the right place
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both Wikipedias for the first orthotopic heart transplant in a dog without artificial circulation; month not recorded. The seven-year survival reported for 1953 rests on en.wikipedia alone, with no reachable clinical write-up of the animal.
stops.campa: He takes out a dog's heart and sets another dog's heart into the space it vacated, in the correct anatomical position, with no machine to carry the circulation while he sews. Nothing exists to buy him time. He has minutes. Two years later one of his transplanted animals is reported to live a further seven years, longer than most of the human recipients of the next two decades will manage, though that claim rests on a single encyclopedia line and no case notes anyone can reach.

stops.name: Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya, artery joined to artery
stops.date_confidence: dates disagree and are left disagreeing. en.wikipedia dates a first mammary-coronary anastomosis to 1952 and a first successful experimental coronary artery bypass to 1953; ru.wikipedia dates the mammary-coronary bypass to 1952 and records a 1988 USSR State Prize for it; Konstantinov 2009 dates a coronary bypass to 29 July 1953.
stops.campa: He joins an internal mammary artery to a coronary artery on a beating animal heart. English Wikipedia dates the first mammary-coronary anastomosis to 1952 and a first successful bypass to 1953; the Russian article gives 1952 for the bypass; Konstantinov dates one to the twenty-ninth of July 1953. The dates disagree. What follows is not disputed. The operation enters human practice in the West more than a decade later. In 1988, thirty-five years after the dog, the Soviet Union awards him a State Prize for it.
suggested_refs: The 1988 USSR State Prize citation for the mammary-coronary bypass
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow, the fifth scientific session, read in Washington
stops.date_confidence: the source article is Meditsinskiy Rabotnik, Moscow, 8 December 1953, byline S. Navashin. The CIA report date cannot be verified because page 1 of the release is stamped 'Page Denied'; an earlier note dated the item 9 June 1954, which is not the article's date. The translator's 'V.F.' is an error for V.P.
stops.campa: He reads a paper at the institute's fifth scientific session, and a notice of it runs in Meditsinskiy Rabotnik over the byline of S. Navashin. Somewhere in Washington an analyst translates the notice, mistypes his initials, and files it. The Central Intelligence Agency is reading the Soviet medical press for the same reason foreign surgeons will shortly start applying for visas to Moscow: the dogs are surviving longer every year, and nobody outside the country can work out how it is being done. The first page of the file, when it is released, is stamped Page Denied.
stops.quote: V.F. Demikhov reported on the transplantation of the heart, lungs, and kidneys in higher animals. As the method of operation used in heart transplantation was perfected, the length of survival of dogs with a transplanted heart was increased from several hours to several days.
stops.quote_source: CIA translation, 'Fifth Scientific Session of Institute of Surgery imeni A. V. Vishnevskiy,' CIA-RDP80-00809A000700180466-4, from Meditsinskiy Rabotnik, Moscow, 8 December 1953 (byline S. Navashin); sanitized copy released 2011
suggested_refs: CIA-RDP80-00809A000700180466-4, declassified translation, CIA Reading Room

stops.name: Bolshaya Serpukhovskaya, the first two-headed dog
stops.date_confidence: month per en.wikipedia (February 1954); ru.wikipedia gives the year alone. Day not recorded. Venue is the Institute of Surgery, where he worked until 1955, not the First Moscow Medical Institute to which an earlier reading assigned the whole series.
stops.campa: He grafts the head and forelimbs of a puppy onto the neck and shoulders of an adult dog, joining the small circulation into the large one so that one heart drives two brains. Photographs of this animal will do more for his reputation abroad, and more damage to it, than every liver and lung he has ever moved. He is not staging a spectacle. He is testing whether a severed head can be kept alive on another body's blood, and it can. The puppy's head wakes, opens its eyes, and drinks milk while the adult body walks about with it.

stops.name: Moscow, an article for a Stockholm newspaper
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the CIA translation, which dates the source article 25 September 1954. The article ran in a Stockholm communist newspaper under Demikhov's name; he wrote it in Moscow and there is no suggestion he traveled to Sweden.
stops.campa: An article under his name runs in a Stockholm communist paper in September, surveying Soviet transplant work for a foreign readership: Sinitsyn's frog hearts, Filatov's corneas that have restored sight to more than five thousand people, reattached limbs in rabbits and goats, transplanted rabbit ovaries whose does bear young normally, and his own dogs carrying a second heart. It reads like a laboratory notebook written out for a newspaper. The Central Intelligence Agency translates the whole of it and files it; the translation is declassified in 2011.
stops.quote: It has not been possible to keep the dogs with two hearts alive for more than 2 1/2 months after the operation.
stops.quote_source: V. Demikhov, article in a Stockholm communist newspaper, 25 September 1954; CIA translation 'Soviet Experiments on Transplantation of Vital Organs,' CIA-RDP80-00809A000700200220-3
suggested_refs: CIA-RDP80-00809A000700200220-3, declassified translation, CIA Reading Room

stops.name: First Moscow Medical Institute, the programme moves
stops.date_confidence: 1955-1960 at the First Moscow Medical Institute (Sechenov) is attested by ru.wikipedia and Konstantinov 2009; month not recorded. The 29-day maximum survival is Konstantinov's; the total of twenty two-headed dogs is ru.wikipedia's; the five-year span to 1959 is en.wikipedia's. Coordinates corrected to Bolshaya Pirogovskaya 2 s1 per OSM.
stops.campa: He moves his laboratory to the First Moscow Medical Institute on Bolshaya Pirogovskaya, and there the head grafts turn from an experiment into a programme. What he is refining is vascular anastomosis under the hardest conditions he can invent, and the conditions he has invented happen to be a chimera. Over five years he produces some twenty two-headed dogs, joining head, forelimbs, and forequarters onto a host animal. They eat, drink, sleep, and are filmed doing it. The longest lives twenty-nine days.
suggested_refs: Sechenov University, Bolshaya Pirogovskaya 2, formerly the First Moscow Medical Institute
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow, a rival in Gorky claims the method
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Meditsinskiy Rabotnik, Moscow, 13 May 1955, Vol 18 No 40, byline 'Prof N. Sinitsyn, Gor'kiy'. The pin is Demikhov's own laboratory, where the technique was practised; Sinitsyn's Gorky is his own place and not a Demikhov stop. An earlier reading of this quote rearranged its clauses into a sentence never written; the wording here is the document's.
stops.campa: In May a rival transplant researcher in Gorky, Professor N. Sinitsyn, publishes a survey of the field and slips into it a single sentence claiming the head graft as his own laboratory's method, with Demikhov's name in the position of borrower. Priority disputes in Soviet science are seldom only about priority; they are how position is contested when there is one funding line and one journal. The claim goes on the record and stays there, and so do the photographs, which are of Demikhov's dogs. The sentence runs to one line, in Meditsinskiy Rabotnik of the thirteenth of May 1955.
stops.quote: In 1954, a communication was published by V.P. Demikhov, who used our method of grafting a second head onto a dog.
stops.quote_source: Prof N. Sinitsyn, Gor'kiy, 'The Problem of the Transplantation of Organs,' Meditsinskiy Rabotnik, Moscow, 13 May 1955, Vol 18 No 40; CIA translation 'Recent USSR Work on Transplantation of Organs,' CIA-RDP80-00809A000700240023-8
suggested_refs: CIA-RDP80-00809A000700240023-8, declassified translation, CIA Reading Room

stops.name: East Germany, the last head transplant
stops.date_confidence: day given in an en.wikipedia image caption: 'The last dog head transplant performed by Vladimir Demikhov on January 13, 1959, in East Germany.' Konstantinov 2009 places his German demonstrations at Leipzig in 1958, so the year is contested. Coordinates are Leipzig, the city Konstantinov names; the caption says only East Germany.
stops.campa: He performs his last head transplant outside the Soviet Union, in East Germany, before an audience of German surgeons. It is the only country beyond the Soviet bloc border he is permitted to demonstrate in. Leipzig will later make him an Honored Doctor of Medicine, a title from a university in a state that has since stopped existing, awarded to a man holding no medical degree at all. The photograph's caption gives the thirteenth of January 1959; Konstantinov puts the German demonstrations a year earlier. What the audience said is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The surviving photograph captioned 'The last dog head transplant, January 13, 1959, East Germany'
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Bolshaya Pirogovskaya, the foreign cameras let in
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The episode is broadly attested by en.wikipedia, which dates Western attention to 1959, but the exact date, the outlet, and the behavioral details vary between retellings; attempts to attest them to a primary Life or newsreel article failed. Month is conventional.
stops.campa: Foreign correspondents are let into the laboratory and allowed to photograph one of the composite animals. The pictures run in the Western press and the dog becomes, in a season, the most famous animal in the Soviet Union after Laika. What the captions carry is not the vascular technique but the image itself: two heads on one body, one of them lapping milk, both tongues moving. The legend that accumulates around those photographs, the two wagging tails, the exact months of survival, changes with every retelling and could not be checked here against a primary article.

segments.name: Sklifosovsky, and the Book That Traveled Instead

stops.name: Sklifosovsky Institute of Emergency Medicine, the last transfer
stops.date_confidence: 1960-1986 attested by both Wikipedias and Konstantinov 2009; month not recorded. The Kovanov reason is ru.wikipedia's alone, en.wikipedia recording the move with no explanation. Coordinates are the institute's own geotag (55 deg 46' 24" N, 37 deg 38' 07" E), reconciling two divergent earlier figures.
stops.campa: He leaves the First Moscow Medical Institute for the Sklifosovsky Institute of Emergency Medicine on the Garden Ring. The Russian article gives a reason: relations with the director, Vladimir Kovanov, have gone bad enough that Kovanov will not let his dissertation go forward to defense. The English article records the move and no reason at all. He will keep a laboratory here for twenty-six years, working on head, liver, adrenal-kidney, esophageal, and limb transplantation. It is the last institution he works in.
suggested_refs: The N.V. Sklifosovsky Institute, Bolshaya Sukharevskaya ploshchad 3, Meshchansky District
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow, Medgiz prints the first monograph in the field
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both Wikipedias; month not recorded and the publisher's address is not sourced, so the coordinates are a declared city-level placeholder.
stops.campa: Medgiz publishes Peresadka zhiznenno vazhnykh organov v eksperimente, Experimental Transplantation of Vital Organs. It is the first monograph the field has, and for a long stretch it is the only one. The word transplantology is his own coinage. This book is what will carry him past the closed borders: surgeons who will never be allowed to meet him can buy him in translation, and within seven years the procedures printed in it are being done on people. Every operation in it is set out with the reasoning behind it, failures included.
suggested_refs: Demikhov, Пересадка жизненно важных органов в эксперименте (Medgiz, Moscow, 1960)

stops.name: Uppsala, elected to the Royal Society of Sciences
stops.date_confidence: Konstantinov 2009 supplies the date, 16 September 1960, for Uppsala; ru.wikipedia lists the honors undated. No reachable source states whether Demikhov traveled to receive any of them, so this stop records an election, not an attested arrival.
stops.campa: The Royal Society of Sciences at Uppsala makes him an honorary member. Hannover does the same, and the Mayo Clinic, and Leipzig gives him the title of Honored Doctor of Medicine. Whether he was ever inside any of those rooms is stated nowhere reachable; a Soviet laboratory biologist in 1960 did not simply take a seat on a plane. The distinctions arrive in Moscow as paper. At home he holds no doctorate whatever, his defense having been blocked, and will hold none for three more years.
suggested_refs: Kungliga Vetenskaps-Societeten i Uppsala, membership rolls for 1960
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow, the South African surgeon at the bench
stops.date_confidence: contested. en.wikipedia's Christiaan Barnard article and ru.wikipedia both date the Moscow visit to 1960, with a second visit in 1963 implied elsewhere; Konstantinov 2009 dates it to 1962 and describes Barnard diverting from a tourist itinerary. No source names the laboratory, so the pin is Sklifosovsky, where Demikhov worked from 1960. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: Christiaan Barnard comes to Moscow and asks to be shown the dogs. He watches Demikhov operate, and he takes notes. The year is disputed: 1960 in both Wikipedia articles, 1962 in Konstantinov's account, where Barnard is a tourist who bends his itinerary to get there, and a second visit in 1963 is implied by some readings and confirmed by none. No source names the laboratory, so the pin is the institute where Demikhov worked from 1960. What Barnard wrote afterward is not disputed, because the letter survives, written in 1997 to the physician who would print it.
stops.quote: was certainly a remarkable man, having done all the research before extracorporeal circulation. I have always maintained that if there is a father of heart and lung transplantation, then Demikhov certainly deserves this title.
stops.quote_source: Christiaan Barnard, letter to Igor E. Konstantinov, 1997, printed in Konstantinov, 'At the cutting edge of the impossible: a tribute to Vladimir P. Demikhov,' Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)
suggested_refs: Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town, 3 December 1967: Barnard's first human-to-human heart transplant, his own stop and not Demikhov's, but the operation the Moscow visit is always read back through
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: New York, Consultants Bureau puts him into English
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and matched city by city by Konstantinov 2009 (New York 1962, Berlin 1963, Madrid 1967); month not recorded. The publisher's office address is not sourced, so the coordinates are a declared city-level placeholder.
stops.campa: Consultants Bureau publishes the book in New York in Basil Haigh's translation, and American surgeons read in English what the Soviet health ministry had let out in Russian two years earlier. The procedures in it have been performed, by one man, on animals, without a heart-lung machine, using instruments he made himself. The book goes where its author cannot. Within five years a South African will do one of them on a living human being, and within a decade coronary bypass is routine in the United States.
suggested_refs: Demikhov, Experimental Transplantation of Vital Organs, tr. Basil Haigh (Consultants Bureau, New York, 1962)
sources: Konstantinov IE, Texas Heart Institute Journal 36:5 (2009)

stops.name: Moscow State University, the defense that needed two votes
stops.date_confidence: contested. en.wikipedia lists a doctoral degree in 1960 and a Doctor of Science in 1963; ru.wikipedia says the 1963 defense before the MSU biology council first yielded only a candidate degree in biological sciences, upgraded to Doctor of Biological Sciences after a second vote. Month not recorded. The awarding body is named by ru.wikipedia, so the pin is MSU rather than a generic city point.
stops.campa: He defends before the biology council of Moscow State University, twenty-three years after graduating from it. The Russian account says the first vote gives him only the candidate degree, the lesser one, and that a second vote is needed before he is made Doctor of Biological Sciences. The English account lists a doctorate in 1960 and a Doctor of Science in 1963 and mentions no difficulty. The two agree on the discipline: the man who has moved more organs than anyone alive is certified in biology. Why a second vote was needed is not stated anywhere reachable.

stops.name: Berlin, the German edition
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia and Konstantinov 2009; month not recorded. Coordinates are a declared city-level placeholder, no publisher address being sourced.
stops.campa: The German edition appears, Die experimentelle Transplantation lebenswichtiger Organe. Madrid follows in 1967 with Trasplante experimental de organos vitales. stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia verbatim: 'Between 1963 and 1965, he also assembled the world's first collection of living human organs for future surgical use.' The span is 1963-1965; earlier notes carried a single 1963 date. Everything else about it is unrecorded.
stops.campa: Between 1963 and 1965 he assembles what is described as the world's first collection of living human organs held for future surgical use. The source says nothing about where the organs came from, who authorized the collecting, how they were kept, or what became of the collection afterward. This is the widest gap in the whole record, and it falls at precisely the point where his animal work would have had to touch human material. It is left here as a gap. Nothing reachable fills it.

stops.name: Sklifosovsky Institute, retirement at seventy
stops.date_confidence: year attested: ru.wikipedia dates the Sklifosovsky laboratory programme 1960-1986 and en.wikipedia gives the same terminal year. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: He retires from the Sklifosovsky Institute at seventy, twenty-six years in the same laboratory. Behind him lie the first heart-lung transplant, the first orthotopic heart transplant, the first isolated lung, the first liver, the first coronary bypass, the head grafts, and the word that names the whole discipline. Ahead of him lie twelve years in a small flat at the edge of Moscow, on a pension, in a country that is about to stop existing. He has never held a license to operate on a human patient. He never applied for one.

stops.name: Moscow, the Order of Merit for the Fatherland
stops.date_confidence: year attested (en.wikipedia: awarded shortly before his death); no month, no ceremony, no venue recorded anywhere reachable, so the coordinates are a declared city-level placeholder.
stops.campa: Shortly before he dies the Russian Federation gives him the Order of Merit for the Fatherland, third class. He is eighty-two, ill, and living on very little in a flat at the edge of the city. The state that hands it over is not the state he worked for; the state he worked for is seven years gone, and its academy, its ministry, and its funding lines went with it. The award arrives four decades after most of the work it recognizes. No ceremony is described in any source reachable here, no date beyond the year, and no photograph of the presentation is named anywhere.

stops.campa: He dies of an aneurysm in his apartment on the twenty-second of November, at eighty-two. Both Wikipedias agree on the date, the age, and the cause. English Wikipedia places the flat on the outskirts of Moscow and gives no street. He dies poor, and largely unvisited by the discipline his book had founded, a discipline that by then moves human hearts as scheduled work. The pin here sits in the middle of the city, which is not where he died. The address is not recorded anywhere reachable.

stops.campa: Eighteen years after the funeral a monument to him is unveiled at the new building of the Shumakov National Medical Research Center of Transplantology and Artificial Organs, out in Shchukino. The date is the twenty-seventh of June 2016, his centenary year. The center is where the country's transplants are done: hearts, livers, lungs, kidneys, moved into human beings as routine work, by anastomoses first cut into dogs by the man now standing in bronze at the door. stops.campa: City Clinical Hospital No. 68, on Shkulyova street in Tekstilshchiki, is renamed for him and becomes the Demikhov City Clinical Hospital. He gets a hospital of his own, sixty years too late to be allowed inside one as a surgeon. Patients are admitted under a name that belonged for eighty-two years to a biologist who operated only on animals, and to whom the medical profession never once handed a scalpel and a human being. A memorial plaque goes up in the administrative block in 2018.
